w: Charles IV ordered construction to begin in 1357, replacing the older Judith Bridge that a flood had wrecked in 1342. Sixteen stone arches, three fortified towers, and a baroque parade of statues from around 1700 - all replicas now, originals moved indoors. It wasn't officially called Charles Bridge until 1870.
_facts: Construction started 1357 under Charles IV, finished early 15th c.
Replaced Judith Bridge (1158-1172), destroyed by a 1342 flood.
516m long, ~10m wide, 16 arches with ice guards, 3 bridge towers.
30 baroque statues added from c.1700, all now replicas.
Only called 'Charles Bridge' since 1870; earlier 'Stone Bridge'/'Prague Bridge'.

w: Bohemia's kings and a run of Holy Roman Emperors are entombed inside this Gothic hulk at the heart of Prague Castle - still the largest and most important church in the country, its main tower reaching 102.8 metres. It's technically dedicated to three saints since 1997; everyone still just calls it St. Vitus.
_facts: Seat of the Archbishop of Prague; Catholic metropolitan cathedral.
Largest and most important church in the Czech Republic; Gothic architecture.
Contains tombs of Bohemian kings and Holy Roman Emperors.
Dimensions 124m x 60m; main tower 102.8m high.
Dedicated only to St. Vitus until 1997, though still commonly called St. Vitus Cathedral.

w: Built for mass synchronized gymnastics on a pitch three times a football field, Strahov once held 250,000 spectators - the second-biggest sports venue ever built, larger than any stadium before or since. No competitive sport since 2019: just a Sparta Prague training ground, occasionally lent out for a concert.
s: Once the biggest stadium ever built, now eerily quiet
_facts: Built for mass synchronized gymnastics; pitch 3x the length and width of a football pitch.
Capacity 250,000 (56,000 seated) - larger than any current or former sports stadium, second-largest sports venue ever.
No longer used for competitive sport as of 2019; training centre for Sparta Prague; has hosted pop/rock concerts.
Located on Petrin Hill overlooking the old city; reachable via the Petrin funicular or trams 22/23/25.

w: A former horse market renamed for Bohemia's patron saint in 1848, then repeatedly filled with crowds ever since - the country's busiest stretch of pavement, and the place people show up when something needs demonstrating, celebrating, or overthrowing. Part of the old town's World Heritage-listed centre.
_facts: Formerly Konsky trh / Rossmarkt (Horse Market); renamed Svatovaclavske namesti in 1848.
Named after Saint Wenceslas, patron saint of Bohemia.
Traditional site of demonstrations, celebrations and public gatherings; busiest pedestrian traffic in the country.
Part of the historic centre of Prague, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

w: Built in 1891 on Petrin Hill, a steel-lattice tower that echoes the Eiffel Tower at a fraction of the scale, originally pulling double duty as an observation platform and a transmission mast. At 63.5 metres it's no giant, but it's stayed one of Prague's best perches for a skyline view over the old city.
s: Prague's pocket Eiffel Tower, built in 1891
_facts: Steel-framework tower, 63.5m tall, on Petrin Hill, built 1891.
Resembles the Eiffel Tower.
Used as an observation tower and a transmission tower.
Today a major tourist attraction.

w: Billed as the alma mater of Czech opera, this is a monument built as much to the survival of the Czech language as to art. Its three companies - opera, ballet, drama - rotate through the historic building along with the State Opera, the Estates Theatre, and the Kolowrat Theatre.
s: The stage that helped save the Czech language
_facts: Historic opera house, known as the alma mater of Czech opera; national monument of Czech history and art.
Consists of three artistic ensembles: opera, ballet, drama.
Ensembles alternate between the historic building, the State Opera, the Estates Theatre and the Kolowrat Theatre.
Repertoire draws on classical heritage and modern authors.
